new_statements.translation: 5.1 Tone. The two phonemic tones are high, marked /´/, and low, which is unmarked. [...] High tone and stress occur simultaneously. In words with more than one high-toned syllable, each subsequent high tone is a little higher than the preceding one. On the first high-toned syllable there occur a somewhat stronger stress and an optional lengthening of the nucleus. [p.114] ... In general, the word has one syllable with a primary stress. The tonal patterns also help to describe the phonological word. The great majority of words fall into one of the following tonal patterns: H, LH, LHL, LHH, LHLL, LHHH. The following patterns are rare: HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL. [p.117]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone (H/L) system; stress is not independent of tone: the primary word stress falls on the first high-toned syllable of the phonological word (with optional lengthening), later H syllables being slightly higher in pitch but less stressed. Since the common word melodies are L H(…) and bare H, primary stress is most often on the second syllable, sometimes the first. Waltz & Waltz 2015 (p.2) state the same distribution morphologically: regular word stress falls on the last syllable of the root (roots mostly disyllabic), tone being marked separately only for tonal minimal pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Klumpp & Klumpp: subsequent high-toned syllables are each slightly higher in pitch but the first H carries the stronger stress. Waltz 2012 dictionary (p.5): if a word or phrase contains more than one stress, the following ones are secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: Waltz & Waltz 2015 p.2: the negative suffix -era [ˈera] and the negative-imperative suffix -é always carry the word stress (exceptions to root-final stress); Waltz 2012 §3.1.4 repeats '-era- lleva el acento de la palabra'. Klumpp & Klumpp list rare initial-H patterns (HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL). Cezario 2025 (after Picanço 2019): root melodies H, HL, LH, LHL with rightward spreading onto toneless suffixes.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'grupo acentual' = phonological word (root plus suffixes, 1-4 syllables typically, up to 7), delimited by stress, tone pattern, the breathy pre-H syllable and potential pause (K&K §7). Examples are citation forms and short utterances. Phrase-level emphatic stress/lengthening is described separately (§8, frase D).
new_statements.identity_note: Both SIL sources (Klumpp & Klumpp 1973; Waltz & Waltz 2015; Waltz 2012) describe 'piratapuyo' as spoken on the Papurí river, Vaupés, Colombia; the Brazilian works (Picanço 2019, Cezario 2025, Balykova 2019) use the autonym Wa'ikhana for the same language (pira1254, ISO pir). No dialect split is claimed in the sources read.

sources.locator: §5.1 'Tono', printed p.114 (PDF p.122) and §7 'Grupos acentuales (palabras fonológicas)', printed p.117 (PDF p.125)
sources.note: Sec. 5.1 'Tono' (printed p.114): two phonemic tones, high (marked) and low; high tone and stress occur simultaneously; the first high-toned syllable carries a somewhat stronger stress and optional lengthening; later H syllables are each slightly higher in pitch. Sec. 7 'Grupos acentuales' (p.117-118): the phonological word generally has one main-stress syllable; common word tone patterns H, LH, LHL, LHH, LHLL, LHHH; rare HH, HL, HHL, HLL, HHH, HLLL (i.e. first H, hence main stress, is usually on the 2nd syllable).

sources.citation: Waltz, Carolyn H. & Nathan E. Waltz. 2015. Una gramática pedagógica del piratapuyo. 1ª ed. SIL International. 80 pp. (SIL archive 63416)
sources.note: 'Notas ortográficas', printed p.2 (PDF p.4): 'El acento regular de la palabra cae en la última sílaba de la raíz; pero por ser patrón regular no es necesario marcarlo. Por ejemplo, waha [waꞌɁa] ir; maca [maAꞌká] pueblo. Unos excepciones son el sufijo negativo [ꞌera] y el sufiijo del mandato negativo [é] que siempre llevan el acento... Para diferenciar entre palabras que son iguales pero que tienen diferentes tonos, se emplea el acento agudo /´/ para marcar el tono alto.' Also: vowel devoicing occurs before a stressed syllable beginning with a voiceless consonant.

sources.citation: Cezario Soares, Bruna. 2025. Verbos seriais em Wa'ikhana (Tukano Oriental): uma abordagem construcionista. Tese de doutorado, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro. 142 pp.
sources.note: pp.65-67 report Picanço (2019: 122-123) second-hand: Wa'ikhana is a tone language, tone aligns with the mora and is lexically distinctive; verbal roots are bimoraic with one of four melodies H, HL, LH, LHL; the root-final tone spreads over toneless suffixes; in serial-verb words the first root's melody governs the whole phonological word (Praat figures). Nothing on stress as distinct from tone.

sources.note: Introducción pp.4-6: high tone written with acute accent, low tone unmarked; stress ('acento (énfasis)') transcribed with [ˈ] before the stressed syllable; if a word or phrase has more than one stress the later ones are secondary; vowel devoicing before a stressed syllable with voiceless onset (peca [pEˈká] 'fuego', weco [weEˈkó] 'loro'). Grammar notes 3.1.4: 'El sufijo -era- lleva el acento de la palabra.' No general placement rule stated (that is given in the 2015 grammar).
